terminal_record.title: AAPD Warned Project 2025 Could Threaten Disability Supports
terminal_record.description_short: AAPD said Project 2025 Medicaid funding and home-care proposals could threaten supports used by people with disabilities.
terminal_record.description_medium: On October 29, 2024, the American Association of People with Disabilities described Project 2025 proposals to shift Medicaid to block-grant or per-capita funding and to limit home- and community-based services. AAPD warned that the proposals could constrain services used by disabled people. This is an attributed warning about proposed policy; the source does not establish later enactment or implementation.
terminal_record.description_long: On October 29, 2024, the American Association of People with Disabilities (AAPD) published a policy brief about Project 2025 and its potential effects on disabled people. In its Medicaid section, AAPD said the plan sought to shift Medicaid toward block-grant or per-capita funding, and proposed narrowing access to home- and community-based services (HCBS). The brief explains that many disabled people rely on Medicaid-funded HCBS to live independently. AAPD warned that restricting Medicaid funding and HCBS eligibility could limit supports for people with disabilities. The warning describes projected consequences if proposals were adopted, not completed government actions. The supplied materials do not establish that the Trump administration abolished ADA accommodations or enforcement, enacted the Medicaid cuts in the prior description, caused a specific number of coverage losses, or forced people into institutions. They also do not show which, if any, of the proposals later became policy. This entry is therefore narrowed to AAPD's attributed 2024 warning about a policy blueprint, without presenting forecasts as realized harm or attributing the blueprint's proposals to a specific administration action.

Project 2025 seeks to turn Medicaid into a block grant program or per-capita funding scheme, which would lead to massive funding cuts by limiting Medicaid funding to a formula that does not consider the specific needs of Medicaid recipients.

source_fact_map.fact: AAPD described a proposal to limit HCBS eligibility and framed potential harms as prospective.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Additionally, Project 2025 proposes limiting HCBS “to serve the most vulnerable and truly needy and eliminate middle-income to upper-income Medicaid recipients” (468) and incorporate work requirements and time limits when receiving Medicaid. This would severely limit the number of Medicaid recipients, many of whom are people with disabilities and who rely on Medicaid and HCBS to live their lives safely, healthily, and independently.

terminal_record.title: Trump Defended Serena Williams After Her 2009 U.S. Open Semifinal
terminal_record.description_short: Trump’s 2009 blog post defended Serena Williams after her U.S. Open semifinal and criticized the backlash she faced.
terminal_record.description_medium: Reporting on Trump’s 2009 blog says he defended Serena Williams after her U.S. Open semifinal against Kim Clijsters. He objected to the backlash and said Williams had apologized enough. The accessible accounts contradict this entry’s claim that Trump called Williams ugly or a bad person; they do not support its golf reference.
terminal_record.description_long: After Serena Williams’ 2009 U.S. Open semifinal against Kim Clijsters ended in a point penalty following a dispute with a line judge, Trump wrote a blog response defending Williams against public criticism. Sportskeeda quotes him saying, “The backlash against Serena has been relentless and she has been treated badly. She has apologized and I think enough is enough.” The same report says he argued that Williams should be allowed to move on and that the line judge should apologize; a separate account by HITC reproduces those remarks. The reporting contradicts this entry’s original claim that Trump called Williams ugly, a bad person, or bad at golf. This corrected record describes the supported event: Trump’s defense of Williams in response to criticism following the 2009 match. The source accounts do not establish the exact publication date of the original Trump University blog post or the number of people who read it. The frozen August date is also incorrect for the U.S. Open incident, which took place in September 2009.
